idiom_name: no inheritance: trait seam + injected double (#[cfg(test)] fake, mockall)
implementation_notes: Rust has no inheritance, so nothing can subclass a struct to override a method: inherent methods are statically dispatched and even trait methods are resolved through the static type (or a chosen trait object). The seam must be dependency injection - a trait defined by the consumer (trait Clock { fn now(&self) -> SystemTime; }) implemented by production types and by a #[cfg(test)] fake, injected as a generic parameter (monomorphized) or as &dyn Clock (object-safe, dynamic dispatch). mockall's #[automock]/mock! generate such doubles when the boundary already is a trait; the classic pattern has no Rust equivalent.
pitfalls: The double replaces the dependency, never the SUT: there is no virtual dispatch on a concrete struct, so a boundary that must be overridden has to move behind a trait first.
dyn Trait requires object safety and adds indirection; a generic parameter avoids the vtable but monomorphizes per double type, which costs compile time and binary size in test builds.
#[cfg(test)] fakes are invisible to integration tests under tests/ (a separate crate compiled without cfg(test)); share the fake through a dev-dependency or a feature instead.
alternative: Extract the boundary behind a trait, inject it as a generic parameter or trait object, and pass a #[cfg(test)] fake or a mockall-generated double (Dependency Injection) - Rust's lack of inheritance leaves no subclass seam to write.
